text.en: Passenger pigeons once numbered in the billions, but the last one, Martha, died on 1 September 1914 — a month after World War I began.
The thylacine was granted protection on 10 July 1936; the last known animal died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September — just 59 days later.
Three months after the Munich Agreement, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin discovered the fission of uranium. The road to the atomic bomb began there.
In November 1922 Howard Carter peered into Tutankhamun's tomb; just over a month later the USSR was founded.
The cheapest toll in Panama Canal history was 36 cents, paid in 1928 by writer Richard Halliburton, who swam it. The fee was set by his weight: 140 pounds.

Gavrilo Princip was not eating a sandwich when the archduke's car arrived; that detail was invented in 2001. The truth: Franz Ferdinand's car took a wrong turn and stalled outside Schiller's delicatessen, right where Princip stood.
On one stretch of the front, the Christmas truce of 1914 was struck for the sake of the post: Belgian soldiers asked the Germans to pass their letters on to families living in occupied Belgium.

Winnie-the-Pooh is named after a real bear brought to London by World War I. In August 1914 Harry Colebourn, a Canadian cavalry vet, bought a cub from a hunter and named her Winnipeg; from 1915 she lived at London Zoo.

The tank is called a tank for secrecy's sake. The British disguised their new fighting machine as a 'water carrier', then settled on the bland word 'tank'. The 'tanks' first went into battle on the Somme in September 1916.
The first countries to put their clocks forward for summer were wartime Germany and Austria-Hungary, on 30 April 1916. Before that, only two small Canadian towns had tried daylight saving, in 1908.

The Spanish flu did not come from Spain. Wartime censors in the warring countries hushed up bad news, while newspapers in neutral Spain reported the outbreak freely, creating the impression that Spain was its source.

Boston was flooded with molasses the day before the US adopted Prohibition. The tank burst on 15 January 1919; the 18th Amendment was ratified on the 16th. The molasses was stored there to be distilled into alcohol.

The first 'face' on television belonged to a ventriloquist's dummy. In 1925 John Logie Baird transmitted the head of 'Stooky Bill', then ran downstairs for a 20-year-old office worker, who became the first person televised in full tone.

Australia and New Zealand have argued for decades over who invented the pavlova. The meringue dessert was named after the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova during or after her tours of both countries in the 1920s.
The first feature-length talkie was mostly silent. The Jazz Singer of 1927 has synchronised sound only in a few scenes of Al Jolson singing and talking; the rest uses title cards.
1928: Fleming came back from holiday to find a mould killing his bacteria, sliced bread went on sale for the first time, and Mickey Mouse made his public debut in Steamboat Willie.

Since its discovery, Pluto has not yet made it even halfway around the Sun. Its year lasts almost 248 Earth years, so having been found in 1930, it will complete its first observed orbit only around 2178.

The Emu War was the idea of World War I veterans. Ex-soldiers turned farmers knew what machine guns could do and asked the defence minister to send some against the birds. The minister readily agreed.
LEGO means 'play well' in Danish. Ole Kirk Christiansen founded the company in 1932 and built its name from the two words leg godt.
Until 1934 people in Turkey were not required to have surnames. A new law made every citizen choose a hereditary one, and parliament gave Mustafa Kemal the surname Atatürk, 'Father of the Turks'.
Hachikō's statue went up while the dog was still alive. The bronze was unveiled at Shibuya Station on 21 April 1934 before a huge crowd; Hachikō attended the ceremony and lived almost another year.
Until 1935 the West called the country Persia. At a Nowruz gathering that year, Reza Shah Pahlavi formally asked foreign delegates to use its own name, Iran.

Adidas and Puma were founded by two brothers. Adolf and Rudolf Dassler made shoes together; Jesse Owens wore their spikes at the 1936 Olympics. In 1949 they fell out: Adolf founded Adidas, Rudolf Puma.
Saudi Arabia struck oil only on its seventh try. Six wells at Dammam yielded nothing commercial; on 3 March 1938 the seventh gushed from about 1,440 m down, and it kept pumping until 1982.

Teflon was found by sawing open an 'empty' cylinder. In 1938 DuPont chemists making a new refrigerant found a cylinder that weighed more than it should; inside was an oddly slippery waxy white coating, the future non-stick pan.
The coelacanth is more closely related to you than to a tuna. Coelacanths are closer to lungfish and four-limbed animals, humans included, than to ordinary ray-finned fish such as tuna or perch.

The ballpoint pen was invented by a Hungarian and launched in Argentina. László Bíró patented it in Paris in 1938; fleeing the Nazis in 1943, he moved to Argentina at the invitation of Argentina's Agustín Justo, who had spotted his pen on holiday.

Velcro was invented after a walk with a dog. In 1941 Swiss engineer George de Mestral came back from a hunt in the Alps covered in burrs and saw hundreds of tiny hooks under the microscope. The name joins velours and crochet.
Casablanca was not filmed in Casablanca. The 1942 film was shot entirely on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank, California, apart from one sequence at Van Nuys Airport in Los Angeles.
The Slinky was invented when a spring fell off a shelf. In 1943 engineer Richard James watched a knocked-off spring 'walk' downwards; in 1945 the toy was a hit at a Philadelphia department store.

The US once banned sliced bread. In 1943 the Agriculture Secretary ordered it as a wartime saving, though not for long. Pre-sliced loaves had gone on sale in 1928, giving English 'the greatest thing since sliced bread'.
During World War II the Oscars were made of plaster. A metal shortage meant three years of painted plaster statuettes; after the war, the Academy let winners swap them for gold-plated metal ones.

In World War II the American psychologist B. F. Skinner trained pigeons to guide bombs. One to three birds in the nose cone would peck at an image of the target on a screen, and their pecks steered the bomb.

The US Army had a unit of artists armed with inflatable tanks. The 'Ghost Army' staged shows for the Germans with rubber vehicles and recorded noise; its ranks included future designer Bill Blass and painter Ellsworth Kelly.

Mike the chicken lived for 18 months without a head. In 1945 a Colorado farmer's axe missed the jugular vein and most of the brain stem. Mike became a celebrity, and his town still holds a Headless Chicken Day.

The first general-purpose electronic computer weighed 27 tonnes. ENIAC was 30 metres long and drew 150 kW; by the end of its career it had 18,000 vacuum tubes and about 5 million hand-soldered joints.
The bikini is named after an atoll used for atomic bomb tests. Frenchman Louis Réard unveiled it in July 1946, four days after a nuclear blast at Bikini Atoll.
The first real computer bug was an insect. On 9 September 1947 a moth was found in a relay of Harvard's Mark II computer and taped into the log with the note 'First actual case of bug being found'.

Cricket's greatest batsman fell four runs short of a perfect average of 100. In his last Test innings in 1948, Australia's Don Bradman was bowled second ball for a duck, and his average stayed at 99.94 forever.

The queen of crime spent part of every year on archaeological digs. After marrying archaeologist Max Mallowan in 1930, Agatha Christie spent several months a year at excavations in the Middle East and used them in her novels.

Vegemite, Australia's national spread, is made from brewing leftovers. It was developed in Melbourne in 1922 from spent brewers' yeast with vegetable and spice additives, and went on sale in October 1923.
The Hollywood Sign began as an ad for a housing estate and read HOLLYWOODLAND. Put up in 1923 as a temporary sign, it was left standing; the last four letters came down only in 1949.

The creator of the Ilya Muromets went on to give the world the helicopter. Igor Sikorsky emigrated to the USA in 1919, and in 1939 flew the VS-300, whose main-plus-tail-rotor layout most helicopters still use.
Britain's King George V was a first cousin of both Nicholas II and Kaiser Wilhelm II. In 1914 Britain and Russia went to war against Germany — two cousins against the third.
Russia's Tsar Tank was tested in 1915, a year before the first British tanks went into battle on the Somme. But the machine with its 9-metre wheels got stuck on its first trial and never saw combat.

The 'sealed train' that took Lenin from Switzerland across Germany in 1917 was not truly sealed: passengers got off, for example to spend a night in Frankfurt. The 'sealed' story was a political cover agreed by both sides.
The October Revolution happened in November: 25 October 1917 in the Julian calendar Russia then used was 7 November in the Gregorian one, so the USSR celebrated 'October' every 7 November.

The first Heroes of the Soviet Union were pilots who flew people off an ice floe. In 1934 the ice crushed the steamer Chelyuskin in the Chukchi Sea, and over a hundred people, two small children among them, waited by an airstrip cleared with shovels.
Chkalov flew over the North Pole to Vancouver — not the Canadian city, but its namesake in Washington State, USA. The nonstop flight from Moscow in June 1937 took 63 hours.
The Kremlin's ruby stars are less than a century old. Double-headed eagles topped the towers until 1935; they gave way to stars set with gems, and in 1937 to today's ruby-glass stars.
The Panama Canal opened in a world already at war. The first ship passed through on 15 August 1914, two and a half weeks after the First World War began, and the opening was a low-key affair.
The idea of the computer and the death of the last thylacine both belong to 1936. Alan Turing described his universal computing machine, and in September the last known thylacine died in Hobart Zoo.

The commander of the Emu War admired the enemy. Major Meredith said a division able to take bullets like these birds could face any army in the world: emus met machine guns “with the invulnerability of tanks”.
A brown bear served in the Polish army in World War II. Wojtek was enlisted as a private so he could board a ship in Egypt, and his company’s badge became a bear carrying an artillery shell.
A pigeon was awarded France’s Croix de Guerre. Wounded and missing a leg, Cher Ami delivered the Lost Battalion’s note in 1918, saving 194 American soldiers from their own artillery.

Murphy's law was born in John Stapp's tests. At Edwards Air Force Base in 1949 engineer Edward Murphy found every sensor wired backwards, and Stapp later repeated his grumble to the press: if anything can go wrong, it will.

Penicillin for millions of soldiers came from a rotten melon. In 1943 a lab in Peoria searching for the most productive mould found it on a mouldy cantaloupe from a local market, and its descendants went into mass production.
Einstein signed over his Nobel Prize before he had won it. Under their 1919 divorce settlement, the money from a future prize was to go to Mileva Marić, and she did get it.

The chain reaction was conceived to spite Rutherford. In 1933 he called the idea of energy from atoms 'moonshine'; Leo Szilard read this in the paper and, by his own account, came up with the nuclear chain reaction that day while crossing a London street.
The famous 'world market for maybe five computers' was probably never said. The line is attributed to IBM chief Thomas Watson in 1943, but no reliable source has ever been found.
The cruiser Aurora never shelled the Winter Palace: on 25 October 1917 it fired a single blank shot as the signal for the assault.
Under Mussolini the trains did not really run on time. Most of the improvement to Italy's railways was done before he came to power in 1922; the famous punctuality was largely propaganda.
